T7.title: Table 7: Cross-Sectional Disagreement by Forecast Horizon
original_notes: Mean cross-sectional standard deviation at short (h+1) and long (h+4) horizons. Ratio = σh+4/σh+1. Positive t- statistics indicate greater disagreement at longer horizons. Paired t-tests (two-sided). Sample: 1999–2023. ∗∗∗p < 0.01.
replication_notes: Computed from raw forecasts, 1999–2023. Sample standard deviations (ddof=1); only quarters with positive SD at both horizons are retained. Paired two-sided t-tests compare long minus short SD; *** p<0.01. All 40 displayed numeric cells match the PDF. Indexing discrepancy: matching the printed Human panel requires current-quarter and three-quarter-ahead forecasts (SPF columns 2 and 5); the AI panel uses one- and four-quarter-ahead forecasts. The PDF labels both panels h+1/h+4.

T9.title: Table 9: AI Forecast Performance During Unexpected Events
original_notes: The table shows the performance of AI forecasters during seven unexpected events occurring immediately before or after the deadline of the SPF survey (days after survey deadline denoted in parenthesis after the event date). The table reports average Z-scores, measuring the difference between the event-period forecast error and the mean forecast error across the full sample, divided by the standard deviation of the full-sample forecast error. Z-scores near zero indicate typical forecast difficulty, while highly negative values (e.g., <-1) would indicate suspiciously accurate predictions suggesting look-ahead bias. The Z-scores are averaged across the relevant variables for each event and across all variables.

T10.title: Table 10: AI Forecast Error Regressions on Knowledge Cut-Off Dummy Variable
original_notes: The table reports OLS regressions of absolute forecast errors of AI forecasters at the one-quarter ahead horizon on a dummy variable, It>Oct 2023, that takes value one after the LLM knowledge cut-off date (October 2023). ∗∗∗p < 0.001, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗p < 0.05. Standard errors in parentheses.

T11.title: Table 11: Forecast Revision Regressions: Human vs AI
original_notes: The table reports OLS regressions of forecast revisions on lagged forecast errors (Error Correction) and distance from SPF consensus (Consensus Tracking). Revisionit is the change in forecaster i’s nowcast from t − 1 to t. SPF regressions use individual forecaster microdata from the Philadelphia Fed (1999–2023). Robust standard errors in parentheses. ∗∗∗p < 0.01.
replication_notes: Recomputed values are the existing qualified reconstruction, which did not recover the published estimator. Stars use the original table’s *** p<0.01 rule.

T12.title: Table 12: Reasoning Categories by Economic Period
original_notes: Percentage of forecaster responses containing each reasoning type. Categories are non-exclusive. Detailed categories: Mechanical (trends, historical patterns, mean-reversion); Policy (Fed actions, fiscal/monetary policy); Model (eco- nomic theory such as Phillips curve, Okun’s law); Event (specific shocks or crises). ECB aggregation: Following ECB methodology, Model-Based combines Mechanical ∪ Model; Judgment-Based combines Policy ∪ Event. All differences between crisis and normal periods are statistically significant (p < 0.001).
replication_notes: The original caption’s claim that all crisis-versus-normal differences have p<0.001 is documentary text; those separate tests were not part of the saved replication audit.

TD15.title: Table D.15: Forecast accuracy (mean absolute errors) of AI-generated and AR(1) SPF forecasts relative to human accuracy
original_notes: The table shows forecast accuracy reported as mean absolute errors of AI-generated SPF forecasts and forecasts implied by an AR(1) model of human SPF forecasts relative to the mean absolute errors of human SPF forecasts. Accuracy is reported for different forecast horizons, with 0, 1 and 4 denoting nowcast, one quarter and four quarters ahead, respectively. For each forecasting horizon, the table boldfaces the lowest MAE relative value between the AI and AR(1) model. The P-val column reports p-values and significance levels for Diebold and Mariano 1999 tests of the statistical significance of the difference between AI and AR(1) forecasts. Significance levels: ⋆ p-value≤0.10, ⋆⋆
